title: Burst Degradation Contracts and Tenant Safety Nets — PRD
content:
Overview:

This doc proposes a complementary model to pure capacity reservation and burst credits: explicit degradation contracts (DCs) paired with tenant safety nets. The idea: when Dedicated pools hit constrained states, we should not only throttle or evict, but have verifiable, contractual degradation profiles we can apply per-tenant so apps degrade predictably (latency, top-k truncation, quantized fallback) rather than fail unpredictably.

Why this is different / motivation:
- Many tenants care less about absolute throughput during short incidents and more about graceful UX: slightly longer tail, truncated responses, or lower model fidelity for a short window.
- Existing approaches (hard eviction, soft-preempt, burst credits) are binary or opaque to customers.
- A Degradation Contract makes tradeoffs explicit: the tenant chooses what kind of degradation is acceptable during bursts and how much of their reserved capacity can be temporarily repurposed.

Goals:
- Define a schema for Degradation Contracts (DC) with orthogonal axes: latency uplift, quality degradation profile, token truncation, fallback model family, and maximum duration per event.
- Implement safety nets that prevent irreversible customer experience damage (e.g., old-model-serving, hallucination spikes).
- Integrate DCs with autoscaler/burst manager so routing, admission, and eviction decisions consider active DCs.
- Provide transparency to tenants (Console + API) with expected degraded-level SLOs and telemetry.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for Reserved Capacity guarantees. DCs are opt-in and intended to improve overall system utilization during exceptional load.
- Not addressing multi-region failover in this RFC — that comes later.

Degradation Contract (DC) model (proposal):
Each DC is a small structured policy the tenant attaches to their Dedicated pool. Fields (initial):
- dc_id: string
- priority: {stable | flexible} (affects fallback order)
- latency_band: {none, +50ms, +100ms, +250ms, +500ms} (expected tail increase)
- quality_profile: {full, topk-trim(1000), topk-trim(256), sample-quantize(8-bit), small-model-fallback} (describes acceptable output quality changes)
- max_event_duration_s: integer (e.g., 900s)
- max_monthly_budget_pct: integer (percentage of monthly reserved capacity that can be converted during DC events)
- emergency_abort_thresholds: list of metrics that if crossed abort DC (e.g., hallucination-rate > 1.5x baseline)
- owner_contact: string

Examples (tenants):
- SearchApp DC: priority=flexible, latency_band=+100ms, quality_profile=topk-trim(256), max_event_duration_s=600, max_monthly_budget_pct=15
- NotebookTenant DC: priority=stable, latency_band=none, quality_profile=small-model-fallback, max_event_duration_s=120, max_monthly_budget_pct=5

How DCs interact with existing burst mechanics:
1) Admission: when pool utilization > threshold and burst credits exhausted, the broker checks DCs for tenants on the waitlist and attempts to apply DCs in priority order before preempting or soft-evicting.
2) Routing: requests from tenants under an applied DC are routed to routes with configured degraded parameters (e.g., quantized kernel, prioritized KV cache reuse, reduced top_k sampling).
3) Accounting: any tokens served under DC are tracked separately (DC_tokens) and counted against the tenant’s max_monthly_budget_pct; an alert is triggered if the tenant approaches limit.
4) Fallbacks: if DC application fails quality gates (see metrics below), the system will roll back to denial/queuing instead of continuing degraded responses.

Tenant Safety Nets (what to protect against):
- Silent quality regressions: require automatic A/B eval sampling during DC to check divergence; if divergence > configured threshold, abort DC and surface logs.
- Billing surprises: preflight simulation visible in console (estimate how many tokens would be consumed in a worst-case DC event).
- Hard outages: ensure DCs cannot allow unbounded overcommit that would cause unrelated tenants to experience total failure.

Autoscaler and controller changes required:
- Policy engine: new DC-aware admission controller that consults active DCs, tenant priority, and pool fairness constraints.
- State machine: DC lifecycle (inactive -> preflight -> active -> cooldown -> expired). Preflight runs a fast checklist (cache-hit expectations, model availability).
- Metrics/events: emit DC_STARTED, DC_ABORTED, DC_COMPLETED, DC_QUALITY_ALERT, DC_BUDGET_WARNING.

Operational runbook (high-level):
- Trigger: pool utilization sustained > 85% for > 60s or sudden spike > 30% within 10s.
- Preflight: controller checks DC suitability (model variants available, KV cache warm). If preflight fails, do not auto-apply.
- Apply: mark tenant state, route degraded configs, notify tenant (console + webhook).
- Monitor: run A/B sampling with golden prompts and produce rolling 1m divergence metric. If divergence > threshold -> abort.
- Cooldown: after event ends, run gradual ramp-back over 30–120s to avoid flapping.

API + Console UX (sketch):
- New REST endpoints: POST /pools/{id}/degradation-contracts, GET /pools/{id}/degradation-contracts, PATCH to update.
- Console: Degradation page per pool showing active DCs, estimated cost impact, QA drift graphs, and a toggle for opt-in auto-apply.

Metrics & telemetry (must have):
- DC_tokens_consumed (per-tenant, per-event)
- DC_quality_divergence (KL, BLEU proxy, or eval score)
- DC_apply_latency_impact (p50/p95 change vs baseline)
- DC_abort_reasons (top reasons)
- DC_usage_vs_budget_pct

SLO / SLA implications:
- DCs are opt-in and do not change the reserved capacity SLA baseline. We will offer optional lower-cost pricing tiers for tenants that enable DCs for part of their capacity; legal review required to expose any SLA changes.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Alpha: internal tenants only (solutions-eng + SRE) to exercise preflight and aborts.
- Beta: selected customers (invites) with clear billing/promises.
- GA: document in pricing, add console flows, train support.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How fine-grained should quality_profile be (top-k vs sampling vs model swap)? Do we expose too many knobs?
- Are customers comfortable signing up for a mechanism that can intentionally degrade model quality? Need legal review of terms.
- Cost allocation: should DC tokens be billed at reserve rate, burst rate, or a blended rate?
- Compatibility matrix: not all models support certain degradation modes (quantized fallback vs smaller model family).

TODOs / next steps:
- Engineering spike: prototype DC preflight and an admission-controller stub (Assigned: Jonah).
- UX: console mockups and billing simulation page (Assigned: Priya).
- SRE: define abort thresholds and safe default values (Assigned: Marco).
- Legal: draft opt-in clause for customer agreements.

Appendix: quick numeric example
- Pool reserved capacity: 100 qps stable.
- Peak event: 500 qps for 30s.
- If 10 tenants allow DCs with max_monthly_budget_pct=10, and DC allows topk-trim(256) with +100ms tail, combined DC_tokens could absorb ~60% of burst (estimate due to reduced compute per request), reducing preemptions from 6 tenants to 1.

Notes to self / meeting fragments:
- 2024-11-12 meeting: SRE liked preflight idea, worried about cache-warm penalty.
- Need a short internal explainer doc for sales + support that explains customer-facing phrasing.

End.
